# Part 1: Quarto Markdown

## Rendering, and rendering errors

Quarto Markdown is a notebook-like tool for writing text and code in one
document. The output can take many forms (the two most common are
HTML and PDF). In this class we produce an HTML report that can then be
converted to PDF.

The Quarto Markdown way to write a link is square brackets for the text the
reader sees, then parentheses for the address:

[TEXT HERE](URL HERE)

> **1.** Please make the line above a working link to Vanderbilt's
> Data Science Institute (https://www.vanderbilt.edu/datascience/)
> with the text reading "Vanderbilt Data Science".

Quarto also lets you use simple HTML styling when you want to change
the appearance of text.

For example:

<span style="color: blue;">TEXT HERE</span>

> **2.** Please make the words "Vanderbilt Data Science" appear in blue
> using the HTML form above, and make the link to the same URL.

Now a case where rendering fails because Python does not recognize a package.
The code below uses `markdown()`, a function from the **`markdown`** package,
to convert Markdown text to HTML. Assume that the package has **not been
installed**.

> **3.** Copy the code below into an executable Python code cell and render
> the document. What did rendering stop with? Please paste the error message
> into the comment below.

```python
from markdown import markdown

markdown("# This is a heading")
```

<!-- YOUR ERROR MESSAGE HERE -->

The error should tell you that Python cannot find the `markdown` package.

One way to fix this is to install the package. In a terminal, run:

```text
python3 -m pip install markdown
```

Then recompile the Quarto document again.

> **What changed? Why did installing `markdown` fix the problem?**

The error message identified the package that Python could not find. Installing
that package makes the `markdown()` function available to the Python environment
used by Quarto.

## Code cells

Python code and its output sit in line with the text through executable code cells
like the one below.

```{python}
print("This is a Python code cell. You can tell by the python label.")
```

Each cell can be run from the notebook interface. Later cells can depend on
objects created by earlier cells, so execution order matters.

### Cell options

Quarto cell options control what a cell does and what the reader sees. The options
below are examples of the kinds of controls you can use.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
#| output: true
#| warning: true
#| error: false

print("Default Python cell options")
```

The Quarto documentation explains these options. Please change the options
on the next four cells so that each does what its instruction says.

> **6.** Make this cell *run* but *not show* its code.

```{python}
print("You can't see me -- John Cena")
```

> **7.** Make this cell *show* its code but *not run*.

```{python}
print("I'm here... but I'm not there")
```

> **9.** Make this figure 5 inches **wide** and 3 inches **tall**,
> **centred** on the page, with the caption
> "Histogram of 100 random numbers from 1 to 10".
>
> **Hint:** You do not need to change the plotting code itself. Quarto
> provides figure options for controlling a figure's **width, height,
> alignment, and caption**. Look for `fig-width`, `fig-height`,
> `fig-align`, and `fig-cap`.
>
> Quarto cell options are placed at the beginning of a code cell and
> start with `#|`.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.random.choice(np.arange(1, 11), size=100, replace=True)
plt.hist(x)
plt.title("Histogram!")
plt.xlabel("RaNdOm NuMbErS")
plt.show()
```

The two cells below demonstrate a Python warning. The first shows the warning;
the second uses a cell option to suppress the warning from the rendered output.

```{python}
import warnings

print("This cell is so fresh and so clean")
warnings.warn("Warning! A warning is not an error; the code still ran.")
```

```{python}
#| warning: false

import warnings

print("This cell is so fresh and so clean")
warnings.warn("Warning! You won't be able to see this warning, though.")
```

### Code that runs off the page

A long line of code is printed as one long line, and a PDF page has
an edge. The cell below is intentionally written as one long line.

```{python}
average_body_mass_by_species = {"Adelie": 3700.66, "Chinstrap": 3733.09, "Gentoo": 5076.02} 
print(average_body_mass_by_species)
```

> **11.** Please rewrite the cell so that no line is longer than
> about 70 characters and the result is the same. One way is to break
> the dictionary across lines after commas; another is to put the
> assignment and the printing on separate lines.

## Equations

Dollar signs produce mathematics. One pair keeps it in the line, like
$x$, and two pairs put it on its own line:

$$x$$

Formal hypotheses are written this way:

$$
H_0: \mu = 0
$$

$$
H_A: \mu \neq 0
$$

We can also align multiple equations inside the same display using
the `aligned` environment:

$$
\begin{aligned}
H_0 &: \mu = 0 \\
H_A &: \mu \neq 0
\end{aligned}
$$

For the notation, see
https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Mathematical_expressions
and, for the symbols,
https://oeis.org/wiki/List_of_LaTeX_mathematical_symbols.

> **12.** The mean of $n$ values $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is their sum
> divided by $n$. Please write it as an equation, with a bar over the
> $x$ on the left, a fraction, and a summation sign with its limits
> ($i = 1$ underneath, $n$ on top).

$$
YOUR \\ EQUATION \\ HERE
$$
